Rin Tin Tin was born in France during WWI. Lee Duncan found him and brought him to America. For years Duncan trained Rinty. First to voice commands in silent films and then to hand signals for "talkies". Rin Tin Tin was enormously popular and his films were so profitable they are given credit for helping Warner Brother studios from bankruptcy. He was nicknamed "the mortgage lifter" by studio big wigs. After Rin Tin Tin died in 1932, he was shipped to France to be buried in a pet cemetery outside Paris. The dog in this film is not Rin Tin Tin but is said to be a descendant.

Noir is a mood that can appear in film in many contexts. Noir appears, in part, in an unlikely place in the "Specter of the Rose", (1946), an early budget effort by director Ben Hecht for the independent and notoriously low-budget Republic Pictures. This is a strange film. It drifts back and forth between a satire and spoof of the world of ballet and high art with its snooty characters and often deliberately stilted dialogue. It was so badly written as to be unbelievable -- nobody had anything to work with. It could only have been made based on Hecht's reputation. rv: Was surprised how good this was. Fast paced, great acting, gripping story. It's hard to believe this was recorded live. I couldn't find one flub or camera error.

The man who wrote the teleplay for this show, Frank Phares, was my uncle - Uncle Frank (my mother's brother). I grew up knowing that he had been a writer/producer in Hollywood, but I didn't get the chance to really know him since we lived outside of Washington, D.C., and he lived in glamorous California (though I recall a couple of visits together at the family home in Texas)! So, stumbling across this actual live TV show of his from 1953 (when I was 5 years old!) is just a real treasure. I hope my kids will watch this and enjoy a piece of their family history.
